en: Having bowed to the supreme lords of Jinas, who are worshipped by the chiefs of the gods and whose afflictions have been shaken off, I shall relate the narrative of the rogue for the sake of enlightening wise people. (Dhutt.
1) There is a city, abounding in a populace of graceful splendor, which surpasses even the city of the gods.
There is a city named Ujjēṇī, the dwelling place of upright people.
To its north is a garden resembling Nandana, filled with thickets of various kinds of flowering shrubs and creepers, and resounded by swarms of bees. (Dhuttaka 2–3)
There, in the garden-house, many hundreds of rogues, engaged in various kinds of crafty activities, happened to have gathered while wandering about.
They were preeminent in deceit and guile, ever intent on improper deeds, and utterly merciless. (Dhutt. 4)

The five types of rogues, who kill the young, the foolish, the old, and those who trust them, and who are solely intent on deception— these are their masters, skilled respectively in incense, collyrium, applications, the *auṣadhani* and *stambhani* spells, and in the varieties of voice and complexion. (Dhuttaka 5–6)
Mūlasiri, Kaṇḍarīya, Elāsāḍha, and Sasā were the [leaders] of Khaṇḍavaṇā;
each of those rogues had five hundred [followers]. (Dhutt.
7) In Khaṇḍavaṇā, there were five hundred female rogues as their retinue.
The lord of them all was Mūlaśrī, renowned throughout the world. (Dhutt.

8) And their time passed during the rainy season, when the paths of the sun and moon were submerged by the waters, and the sky resounded with rainbows, lightning, thunder, and sea-monsters. (Dhutt. 9)
And during that seven-day period of foul weather, when the fields, wells, and ponds were filled on all sides,
and the streets were difficult to traverse due to the thick mud and slush;
at such a time as that, those rogues were struck by the cold and rain.
"Tormented by hunger, they say there: 'Who will give us food? (Dhutt.
11) Then Mūladeva says: "Whatever has been heard or whatever has been personally experienced by each, let him tell all of that to these rogues who have gathered together. (Dhutt. 12)
"He who would not believe that it is a false statement must provide food and drink for all the assembled swindlers. (Dhutt.
13) But he who [relies] on words arising from the hearing of the ancient *Bhārata*, *Rāmāyaṇa*, and so forth...
Having justified that speech, he caused the great caravan to have confidence. (Dhutt.
14) "That leader of rogues is highly intelligent and skilled in the arts; let him not give anything to anyone," thus was it said by Mūladeva. (Dhutt. 15)
They all said, "So be it; that is very well spoken by you.
But he replied, "However, you must tell first what was experienced by you. (Dhutta.
16) Then Mūladeva said: "That which was experienced by me in my youth—"
Listen attentively to this as it is told with sound reasoning. (Dhutt.
17) In my youth, longing for the attainment of desired pleasures and prosperity, I set out for a long time toward the house of a master for the sake of shelter from the rain. (Dhutt. 18)
With umbrella and water-pot in hand, carrying my bedding, I was traveling along the road when I saw a magnificent elephant approaching,
as large as a mountain, intoxicated and trumpeting like a thundercloud, its temple-glands bursting open. (Dhuttaka 19)
Seeing the lord of the forest elephants, my limbs trembling with fear, I thought, "Alone and without refuge, where shall I hide?
Then, terrified by the fear of death, I suddenly entered a water-pot. (Dhutt. 20–21)
Then that rutting elephant, with its trunk uplifted and eyes red with rage,
followed the path of the middle [of the road] and quickly rushed toward the water-pot.
Then I, bewildered by fear, looked about in all directions for a way out.
Having enchanted the elephant with my water-pot for six months, I emerged from its neck;
the elephant, following in my wake, became stuck at the tip of its tail within the opening of the pot-neck. (Dhutt. 23–24)
And I too, moreover, see before me the Gaṅgā, with its dancing waves,
laughing with masses of foam, its banks and summits scarred by the tusks of wild elephants—
abounding in thousands of billows, and surrounded by fish, crocodiles, sharks, and tortoises. (Dhuttakalpa 25)
The heart of a young woman is unfathomable like the ocean, its further shore very distant.
Finding no other path, I then swiftly crossed over Bhārahī with my arms—she who carries away the flow of arrows—just as one crosses a broad river. (Dhuttakkhāna 26–27)
Enduring the hardships of hunger and thirst, I carried the Lord’s alms-bowl on my head for six months while standing under a rain-cloud.
Having held the bowl and having prostrated myself before Mahāsena, I departed. (Dhutt. 28)
"I have arrived at Ujjain and have met with you. (Dhutta 29) "Therefore, if this is true, then convince me with reasons; but if you consider it false, then give food to the rogues. (Dhutta 30)
Then Kaṇḍarīka said: "Who would say that you speak an untruth, when a man knows the Mahābhārata, the Purāṇas, and the Rāmāyaṇa? Mūladeva replied: "How did that elephant die in Kuṇḍiyā?"
"How did you wander for six months in that water-pot, O forest elephant? (Dhutt.
32) "How did I emerge from the water-pot through its minute opening, and how did that forest elephant become caught on the tip of my hair as he emerged? (Dhutt. 33)
"How did I cross the Ganges, its far shore so distant, by means of my arms?
How was the stream of water sustained for six months by me, hungry and thirsty?
Then Kaṇḍarīka says: "That which is heard in the Purāṇa of Bhārata..."
If all that is true, then your words are also true. (Dhutt.
35) As for what you say—"The elephant, the water-pot, and I too have died"—listen here to a statement well-known among the gods as a means of proof. (Dhutt. 36)
From the mouth of Brahmā came the Brahmins, from his arms the Kṣatriyas, it is said, and from his thighs the Vaiśyas;
from his feet came the Śūdras. (Dhutt.
37) If all this multitude of people were born from the body of Brahmā...
How is it that you do not even fit within a water-pot, yet you have taken possession of the entire forest? (Dhutt.
38) Moreover, Brahmā and Viṣṇu, though both running upwards and downwards for a thousand celestial years, did not reach its end. (Dhutt. 39)
"How could that linga of such great size have been fashioned upon Uma's body?
If an elephant is fashioned out of a small vessel, what is the fault in that? (Dhutt. 40).
Furthermore, this is heard: it was stated by the sage Vāsava in the Bhārata.
Just as in the middle of a bamboo stalk a hundred kīyaga brothers were born (Dhutt.
41). A bamboo is called *kīya*; those born therein are called *kīyaga*.
How did their origin come about? [It was] from the chief queen of King Virāḍa. (Dhutt. 42)
She too had no son; therefore, she began to propitiate a certain seer in a hermitage.
He also prepared that sacrificial porridge (*caru*) for her.
And by that seer she was told: "Place this sacrificial porridge in a thicket..."
"Eat, and be joyful in heart; there you shall have a hundred sons.
Having eaten that [food] in the bamboo thicket, she went to her own home.
After some time, a supreme sage named Gargali arrived there.
Having entered the bamboo thicket, he was practicing penance; there, in a lotus pond, a celestial nymph was seen by the seer while bathing, naked.
A drop of semen fell from the agitated [seer] into the stalk, and thus the first *kīyaga* (a type of insect) was produced. (Dhutt. 46)
He became endowed with the strength of nine thousand elephants at the first drop. (Dhutt.
47) The more the sage gazes upon the celestial nymph’s exquisite form and beauty, the more the second drop oozes out, from which hundreds of monkeys are born there. (Dhutt. 48)
Having set aside the bamboo tubes, the sage returned to his own abode;
that very king constantly guarded the bamboo thicket. (Dhutt. 49) With her entire body covered, she was seized by the queen, whose mind was filled with joy.
That hundred of sons born of the reed is called "reed-born" (nālī-samuppanna). Dhutt. 50.

If, O Mother, that hundred of brothers born of the bamboo is "born of the bamboo" (vaṃsa-samuppanna) for those who buy it, then why did you not measure that entire quantity of forest-grown [bamboo] into the water-pot? Dhutt. 51.

If for a thousand years Gaṅgā was captivated by the charms of Jaḍā, and if for six months Hari was utterly infatuated with Kuṇḍikā, then the forest-dweller [the Buddha] is truly a fool. (Dhuttaka 52) The elephant is stuck to the very tip of a hair, while I have emerged; how indeed [could he be compared]?
Listen to that which you say, the word derived from ancient scripture:
Viṣṇu is the creator of the world; it is said that he [created] this world in a single ocean, devoid of space, earth, wind, moving beings, stationary things, water, and fire. (Dhutt. 53–54)
When the world of men, gods, and animals has perished, and is bereft of stars, moon, and sun,
the Infinite One, whose nature is inconceivable, lies upon his bed of water and performs penance.
It is said that from the navel of that [Lord], who is seated upon a lotus, Brahmā emerged from the interior of a lotus.
Even one who has emerged with staff and water-pot in hand may have his lotus-stalk caught in the mud. (Dhutt.
56) In the same way, if you, having emerged from the neck of the water-pot, were to cling to the tip of a hair on an elephant even while moving like a gait, then what is improper in this? (Dhutt. 57)
And as for what you say, O mine of virtues, that I have emerged from the neck of a water-pot—listen here to a statement famous in the *Bhārata* as a means of conviction:
"For a thousand divine years, Brahmā performed penance in the forest. (Dhutt. 58)
Then the hosts of gods were agitated and asked, "How could there be an obstacle for him? (Dhutt.

59) Then the Lord of the Suras, who was lustful for women, replied: "At the marriage of the Lord of Beasts, he was appointed to the fire-rite; having seen Uma with her garment slipped off... (Dhutt. 60)
Agitated, he discharged semen and shook his garment;
then the seed fell into the jar, and the Master Dōṇā was conceived. (Dhutt.
61) Even by women of such beauty, he would have been disturbed.

Who, indeed, has not been shaken by women, except for the Great Hero, the Jina? Dhutt.62 Gautama, Vasiṣṭha, Pārāśara, Jamadagni, Kāśyapa, Aghastya, and I myself, the Lord of the Gods, Hara, and Hari—the most excellent in the three worlds—[have all been moved]. Dhutt.63
Moreover, even in this world, there have been men of such great power, renowned as treasuries of asceticism,
who, struck by the arrows of Love, were made to obey the commands of women.
Therefore, Tilottamā, the most excellent among the celestial wives, must go quickly.
Then she,
having assumed a charming disguise and having received a message from the words of the Lord of the Gods,
went before the Lord and displayed a divine dance. (Dhuttakkhāna 65–66)
Tumbling as they walk slowly, their graceful movements slowed by their dangling necklaces;
their delicate silk garments trembling upon their breasts covered in thick, smooth ointment;
their slender bodies adorned with playful gestures, and the pair of vine-like arms revealing side-long glances. (Dhūrtaviṭasaṃvāda 67)
She shines as she dances, like a campaka creeper swayed by the wind. (Dhutt.
68) Seeing her dancing, Brahmā became as if single-sensed; with eyes unblinking, he gazes on her, having abandoned the activity of his remaining senses. (Dhutt. 69)

Having understood his state of mind, she— charming with her graceful form, adorned with various ornaments, and standing at his right side— vanished. Then, no longer seeing her, the brahmin was struck in his heart by the one known as the Mind-born (Kāma).
Having seen that, one who possesses craving makes a seed;

then, with the word "from here" (etto), he makes the third, and with the word "beyond" (avareṇa), the fourth; with the word "upward" (uttareṇaṃ), he makes the fifth word directed upwards as it flies up. (Dhutt. 71–72)
Then, while he was thus negligent and his mind fixed on Tilottamā,
that face was suddenly struck by the fifth nail (nail-mark) of Rudra with his hand. Thereupon Brahmā became enraged and, with his right hand...
On his forehead, he wiped away the sweat born of incomparable rage.
There, a powerful being named Seyakuṇḍalī was born; by the command of Brahmā, that being cast out the mixture (of the two). (Dhutt. 74–75)
Terrified by fear and seeking refuge, that monkey reached the vicinity of the mendicants;
there, having been told "Give alms," he immediately exposed his own head with its veins visible. (Dhutt. 76)
The skull of the Brahmin’s head was cast down by Rudra;
even in ten thousand years, it could not be filled by that stream of blood, for that blood had been sucked out by the finger of the Lord of Beasts alone. (Dhutt. 77–78)
When the skull of the Brahmin was [placed] upon his head and Keshava’s blood was on his fingers, Rudra became joined with the three [deities].
Directed by Rudra, he fought against Shvetakundali. (Dhūrtākhyāna 79)
As they were fighting, a thousand years passed by. Then, having captured both of them, all the foremost gods gathered together;
one man was given to Śakra, and the second was handed over to Sūra. (Dhutt. 80–81)
In the age of Bharata, he was addressed for the sake of the Bharata war;
at the time of Bharata’s downfall, he was brought down into the world of men.
Then, when the time had arrived, the hero [was born] to Kuntī, intoxicated by her beauty. *Dhūrtākhyāna* 82.
The bodily union produces that embryo within her womb. (Dhutt.
83) O Kuṇḍigīvā, since Karṇa emerged from Kuntī’s ear with his armor already fastened and bound, why do you not emerge from the base of the neck of the *kuṇḍi*? (Dhutt. 84)
"You ask me how I crossed the Gaṅgā, whose further shore is so difficult to reach;
listen now to what occurred here in the *Rāmāyaṇa* to produce conviction. At the request for news of Sītā, the son of the Wind was commanded by Rāghava. (Dhutt. 85)
Having crossed the great ocean by means of his arms, he arrived at the city of Laṅkā. (Dhutt.
86) When Sītā was seen, she was delighted to hear the news of her husband’s return and asked, "O Hanumān, how did you cross the ocean? He replied: (Dhutt. 87)
And there is a verse on this point:

"O Goddess, by your grace, by your grace, and by the grace of your husband, and by the grace of your virtuous father, I have crossed the ocean as easily as one crosses a cow's footprint. (Dhutt. 87–1)
If he crossed that great ocean, so difficult to traverse, as an animal, then, O best of men, why could you not have crossed the Gaṅgā? (Dhutt.
88) As for what you say—how indeed was the stream borne on my head for six months?
In this matter as well, hear my reason, a statement derived from the tradition of the *Dīyāi* [the *Devīpurāṇa*]. (Dhutt.
89) It is said that for the sake of the world’s welfare, the Gaṅgā was entreated by the foremost of gods: "Descend from heaven to the realm of men. Then she replied: (Dhutt. 90)
"Who is able to hold me as I fall? the Lord of Beasts (Śiva) said.
"I shall hold you. Then she fell and was caught by the Lord of Beasts upon his head.
Why then do you not bear the stream of tears upon your head for six months? (Dhutt.

92) You are a superior man, perfected in the virtues of wisdom and traditional learning; your fame has spread abroad, and you are a great soul renowned throughout the world of living beings. (Dhutt. 93)
Thus addressed, Mūlaśrī said to Kaṇḍarika: "Tell me now what you have seen, what you have heard, and what you have experienced here. (Dhutt. 1)
Then Kaṇḍarīka said: "In my youth, I was full of immodesty; being difficult to control for my mother and father, I departed from home out of anger.
While wandering about, I arrived at a village situated in a foreign land. (Dhutt. 2)
Crowded with cows, buffaloes, goats, sheep, donkeys, and camels, it was joyful;
beautified by parks, gardens, and groves flourishing with flowers and fruits, it was as delightful as Ayodhyā, teeming with many hundreds of houses. (Dhuttaka 3–4)
In its very center, I saw a banyan tree, enchanting to the mind, appearing like a mass of clouds, a dwelling place for thousands of birds.
And beneath it was a Yakṣa with eyes like lotus petals, endowed with all virtues. (Dhutt. 5)
That yakṣa, having manifested his miraculous power, grants boons to those who seek them.
(Dhutt. 6) The festival of that yakṣa proceeds, crowded with many people;
there the folk come in a state of joy, carrying incense, offerings, and flowers in their hands. (Dhutt. 7)

Having bathed, groomed himself, and eaten, his body adorned with all ornaments, wearing various garments and anointed with sandalwood paste—filled with curiosity, I then approached that great multitude of people. (Dhutt. 8)
Having bowed before the Yakṣa, while I was enjoying myself, I saw horses [running].
(Dhutt.9) Then, heavily armed, with armor fastened and weapons and missiles grasped, a great multitude of thieves fell there, raising a tumultuous clamor. (Dhutt.10)
Then that entire population—both young and old, including women, along with the herds of cattle and accompanied by horses—went all together toward Vāluṅka.
There too, the people were delighted in mind, watching those horse-slayers as they sported. (Dhutt. 11)
The thieves also retreated, saying, "The village has been ruined.
Just then, a herd of cattle, grazing there quite confidently, arrived;
then, from one cow, a mass of dung suddenly fell. (Dhuttakālāpa 12–13)
She was struck by a snake, and he, in turn, was crushed by a cart;
she remained right there, hidden beneath a vast and lofty banyan tree.
Only the trunk of that tree stood there, as did the king’s intoxicated elephant.
Thinking, "A banyan tree has grown at the foot of the swing," [he climbed up];
when the foot was pulled back, the noble elephant was dragged along, trumpeting loudly, while the group of cowherds cried out, "Someone has lifted up a bull! (Dhutt. 15–16).
Hearing their sound, the warriors, skilled in hearing sounds,
arrived with bows and arrows in hand, raising a tumultuous roar;
yet her wings were severed by them, and her head was struck down by skillful elephants.
Lamenting, she fell upon the surface of the earth like a mountain peak;
and when her belly was slit open by the king, a vast serpent was seen within, fallen upon the ground like the axle-end of a wagon. (Dhutt. 18–19)
Then the lord of men said: "Let this vast python be split open;
let there not be even a human or an animal within its belly. (Dhutt.
20) Then, when the belly was split, that great-bodied female serpent was seen.
Within her belly as well, he saw a charming little pouch.
"Hī hī! Oh, what a large pouch! the king exclaimed, while the horses stood there, their trunks raised high, having finished their play. (Dhutt. 21–22)

And as that multitude of people proceeded to go out from there through the sand like a swarm of moths emerging from a chaff-hollow, all those four-footed folk then bowed down to the lord of men. (Dhutt.
Having gone to my respective places, I too have arrived at this city. (Dhutt.
24) This has been experienced by me directly right here in the human world; let him who does not believe me give food to rogues! (Dhutt. 25)
Then Elāsāḍha said: "We swear it; there is no doubt at all.
Kaṇḍarīya replied: "How was the village Cibbhaḍa destroyed? Elāsāḍha replied: "This is a matter seen in the ancient *Bhārata* scriptures. (Dhutt. 26)
Why has the Viṣṇu Purāṇa not reached the path of your ears? (Dhutt.
27) Previously, this world was a deep, vast, single ocean of water, devoid of the five great elements; therein was an egg. (Dhutt. 28)
Churning through the succession of aeons for a very long time, it split and became two parts; one half became the earth.
Therein lies the entire world, consisting of gods, asuras, hell-beings, humans, and quadrupeds. (Dhutt. 29)

If it were possible [to deceive], why indeed would the village not be able to deceive a jackal? Furthermore, this is heard: on the mountain Araṇī, the son of Dharma (Yudhiṣṭhira) was told by Makaranda, who was joined by another, that which had been experienced by him. (Dhutt. 30–31)

At the time of the end of the eon, when the world had become a single ocean due to the deluge, he, wandering through the succession of currents in the midst of that flood, beheld [the world] with its mobile and immobile beings gone, and the realms of gods, humans, and animals vanished. (Dhutt. 32)
"This world is a single ocean, fallen away from the five great elements. (Dhutt.
33) In such a world as this, he sees a tree of growth—lofty like Mount Mandara and vast like the great ocean. (Dhutt. 34)
On a heap of chaff lay his bed; there the boy remained, delightful to the mind, with a fully developed body and limbs, soft, supple, and well-proportioned. (Dhutt.
35) His hand was extended by the sage, who said, "Come, come, my child."
"Climb onto my shoulder; you shall not die in this flood.
Having taken him by the hand, that seer then looked into his belly and saw the entire world, with its mountains, forests, and groves. (Dhuttakkhāna 36–37)
For a divine thousand years, that seer wandered within the womb, yet he did not reach the end; the best of seers emerged from there. (Dhutt.
38) If the mother [beholds] the world with its gods, asuras, and humans within the belly of the child...
"How indeed could the village not fit within that small intestine, Kaṇḍarika?
"In the belly of the swing-maker was a python; in its belly was the intestine; and there too was a multitude of people. How did they fit? Listen to this. (Dhutt. 39–40)
Keśava was conceived in the womb of Devakī, whose waist could be grasped by a fist;
within his belly [resided] the earth with its mountains, forests, and groves.
Then Kaṇḍarika says: "In the midst of raw meat, cattle, snakes, and so forth..."
"Since I am still living, how could I not be dead? Convince me of this. (Dhutt.
42) And Elāṣāḍha says: "On that very day you departed;
how then, O Earth, do you not perish while the son of Vasudeva remains within your womb? (Dhutt. 43)
In this belly, various kinds of trade, many types of undertakings, weddings and marriages, as well as festivals and births, all take place.
But how could this victory exist even in the belly, wherein that which was described [in the previous verse] resides? (Dhutt. 44)
It is said that in former times there was a dispute between Brahmā and Keśava.
Brahmā declared, "I am the creator," because this fourfold world emerged from his speech, arms, thighs, and feet. (Dhuttakkhāna 45–46)
Ananta replied to that Brahmin with humorous words:
"It is not fitting for you to speak such things to me, who am like a servant.
[I am] one whose lips are the clouds, whose tusks are the mountains, and whose tongue is the ocean. (Dhutt. 47)
"Enter my belly so that you may see the earth with all its splendors. (Dhutt.
48) "O Brahmin, since you were born from the navel of me who lay upon the waters, it does not befit you to speak such things in the presence of your elders. (Dhutt. 49)
Moreover: By whose power they were made to blossom, yet those very same lotuses, now self-conceited, how ungrateful they are as they mock the moon! (Dhutt. 50)
Then Kaṇḍarīka said: "Where have you heard in the ancient scriptures that there was such a large cart whose belly could hold such a quantity?
Elāsāḍha replied: "I saw it at the svayaṃvara of Queen Dōvaī."
Just as it is said that mountains, serpents, and even fire have entered the bow [of the King]. (Dhutt.
52) The bow of the two-legged lord of men is exceedingly large and protected by a deity; he who has climbed upon it pierces the left eye with a needle. (Dhutt. 53)

Having strung that bow with effort, however, by Ayatta.
Then Kṛṣṇa placed Garuḍa, the Nāgas, the elephants, the conchs, the discus, the plow, the pestle, and Mount Mandara and Meru [upon it]. (Dhutt. 55–56)
